subject: Critical Thinking
title: Motivated Reasoning: Thinking Backwards from Conclusions
description: A short lesson to help you apply Motivated Reasoning: Thinking Backwards from Conclusions.

hook.text: You don't believe X because of the evidence. You found the evidence because you already believed X.

buildup.text: Motivated reasoning: unconsciously selecting, interpreting, & remembering evidence to support conclusions you want to.

discovery.text: Kunda proved it: when people want a conclusion, they search for supporting evidence.

twist.text: Smart people are better at it — they have more sophisticated tools for constructing plausible-sounding justifications.

climax.text: Jonathan Haidt's metaphor: reasoning is the 'press secretary' – it rationalizes decisions the 'president' already made.

punchline.text: You're not reasoning toward truth. You're lawyering for your side.

quiz.question: What is motivated reasoning?
options: Unconsciously selecting evidence to support desired conclusions

details.summary: Motivated reasoning occurs when people start with a desired conclusion and work backward to construct justifications for it. Unlike honest reasoning that follows evidence, motivated reasoning selects evidence to fit a predetermined answer.
details.whyItMatters: Motivated reasoning makes intelligent people defend wrong positions more skillfully, turning intellect into a tool for self-deception.
takeaways: Intelligence does not protect against motivated reasoning
Emotional investment in a conclusion drives biased analysis
Separating your identity from your beliefs reduces the effect

faq.question: How is motivated reasoning different from confirmation bias?
faq.answer: Confirmation bias passively filters information to match existing beliefs, while motivated reasoning actively constructs arguments to defend a conclusion you want to be true.

faq.question: Why are smarter people sometimes more susceptible to motivated reasoning?
faq.answer: Higher intelligence provides better tools for constructing convincing rationalizations, making it easier to find sophisticated arguments for whatever you already believe.
